metaDescription: Six heavy-duty plant caddies rated from 264 to 600 pounds compared on locking casters, caster count, frame material and adjustable versus fixed bases.
introParagraphs: Heavy-duty is a loose term on plant caddies, and the gap between a 264 pound wooden tray and a 600 pound metal platform is the gap between a mid-size ficus and a concrete urn. What separates the serious ones is not the headline rating alone but how many casters share the load, how many of them lock, and what the frame is made of.

This lineup runs from a 264 pound acacia wood pair to a 600 pound 22 inch metal platform, with caster counts from four to nine and one adjustable design that expands from 21 to 30 inches. We evaluated each pick on its stated specs and features rather than on any hands-on trial, and we flag where a listing omits a detail.
Start with a number you can measure: the loaded weight of your heaviest pot and the diameter of its base. Both matter more than any badge in this guide.

products.name: MEADOMINGLE 22 in Round Metal Plant Caddy, 600 lb
products.description:
The MEADOMINGLE is a 22 inch round metal platform rated for 600 pounds, the highest rating in this guide. The listing describes thickened heavy-duty metal, a rust-proof finish and a platform that fits planter pots up to 24 inches. Its wheels are industrial-grade, with two swivel casters and two lockable casters.

The size and rating make it the pick for oversized urns, large ceramic pots and small trees that no light caddy can handle. The platform is large enough that a pot sits on it with plenty of margin, which helps stability. The tradeoff is that only two of the four casters lock, so on a slope you should confirm the lock holds before you walk away.

A 22 inch metal platform is bulky to store and heavy to lift empty, so plan where it will live. Compared with the 500 pound GLISWAM, it adds 100 pounds of rating but is fixed in size rather than adjustable. Compared with the 390 pound Parsagi at 14 inches, it is much larger and has half the casters locking instead of all of them. A realistic scenario is a 20 inch ceramic urn holding a small citrus tree that you roll into a garage each winter.
products.bestFor: Oversized pots and small trees that need the highest rating and a big platform.
pros: 600 lb rating is the highest here
22 in platform fits pots up to 24 in
cons: Highest price rank in the lineup

products.name: GLISWAM 21-30 in Adjustable Metal Plant Caddy
products.description:
The GLISWAM is an expandable plant caddy that adjusts from 21 to 30 inches to fit square, rectangular and round planters. The listing states a 500 pound capacity, a reinforced cross-braced metal frame and four locking casters that roll silently on hardwood, tile or carpet. It is described as suited to ceramic, concrete or oversized pots.

Adjustability is the main reason to choose it, because one caddy can serve several pots as the plant grows. The cross bracing is meant to keep the frame from flexing under a heavy load. The tradeoff is that an adjustable frame has more joints than a solid tray, so tighten every fastener fully and recheck it after the first few moves.

Because the caddy is an open frame rather than a solid disc, check that the base of your pot rests on the rails evenly. Compared with the 600 pound MEADOMINGLE, it has 100 pounds less rating but locks on all four casters and adjusts to fit. Compared with the fixed 16 inch KEDSUM at 440 pounds, it is larger in range and rated higher. For a rectangular planter box, the expandable frame is the only pick here that can follow its shape.
products.bestFor: Large square or rectangular planters and growing plants that may need a bigger base later.
cons: More joints to check than a solid tray
Open frame needs even support under the pot

products.name: TECHYANG 20 in Heavy-Duty Plant Caddy, 500 lb
products.description:
The TECHYANG is a 20 inch round caddy rated for 500 pounds. The listing says it is made from heavy-duty, UV-resistant plastic and carries nine wheels. It is described as working with pots and planters of any shape and size.

Nine wheels spread the load across many contact points, which makes rolling a heavy pot smoother and lowers the pressure on any single wheel. UV-resistant plastic suits a sunny patio and will not rust. The tradeoff is that the listing, in the bullets we have, does not state how many of the nine wheels lock, so check the product page.

Plastic is lighter than metal, which makes the empty caddy easier to handle. Compared with the MEADOMINGLE at 600 pounds and 22 inches, it is a little smaller and lower rated but plastic and many-wheeled. Compared with the 440 pound KEDSUM at 16 inches, it offers a larger 20 inch diameter and a higher 500 pound rating, though the KEDSUM states its five ball-bearing casters. A practical use is a big shrub in a resin-style planter that sits in full sun all summer.
products.bestFor: Large patio planters where rust resistance and smooth rolling matter.
cons: Lock count not stated in bullets
Plastic is less rigid than metal

products.name: KEDSUM 16 in Galvanized Steel Plant Caddy, 440 lb
products.description:
The KEDSUM is a 16 inch caddy made of galvanized steel with an anti-rust coating and a carbon steel frame rated for 440 pounds. The listing counts five heavy-duty industrial casters with double ball bearings and mentions an edge design and anti-slip surface. It is described as heavy-duty for indoor and outdoor use.

The caster hardware is the highlight, because ball-bearing casters roll more smoothly under load than plain ones. Five casters distribute weight well, and galvanizing should help against outdoor moisture. The bullets do not say how many casters lock, so check the product page before buying for a slope.

A 16 inch size suits mid-to-large pots. Compared with the Parsagi 14 inch at 390 pounds and five locking casters, the KEDSUM carries 50 pounds more and is larger. Compared with the 600 pound MEADOMINGLE, it is smaller and rated lower but more compact to store. On a wet deck, galvanizing and an anti-rust coating are worth more than a high rating alone.
products.bestFor: Mid-to-large pots needing smooth-rolling industrial casters.
pros: Five casters with double ball bearings
Edge design to hold the pot

products.name: Parsagi 14 in Metal Plant Caddy, 390 lb
products.description:
This Parsagi caddy has a 14.48 inch outer diameter, a 13.58 inch inner diameter and five locking casters. It is rated for 390 pounds and comes with a basic wrench for assembly. The listing says the wheels are steel with bearing balls and locking brakes.

Five locking casters is a rare combination, because it means every wheel can be braked once the pot is in position. That is the most secure setup in this guide for slopes and busy floors. The tradeoff is capacity, which is lower than the 500 and 600 pound picks, and the need to assemble the caddy with the wrench.

The 13.58 inch inner diameter fits many large pots. Compared with the KEDSUM at 440 pounds and an unstated lock count, the Parsagi gives up 50 pounds of rating but states five locking casters. Compared with the 600 pound MEADOMINGLE, it locks every wheel and is far smaller. For a heavy ficus in a living room with a slightly sloped floor, all five wheels locked is the setup that lets you walk away.
products.bestFor: Heavy pots on slopes or busy floors where every wheel should lock.
cons: Lower rating than the 500 lb picks

products.name: IDZO 14 in Acacia Wood Plant Caddy, 2 Pack
products.description:
The IDZO comes as a two-pack of fully assembled 14 inch acacia wood plant caddies, each rated for 264 pounds. The listing says it has 360 degree lockable casters and suits indoor and outdoor use. It is described as a sleek option for large pots.

Acacia is a dense hardwood, and the two-pack arrives ready to use, which is a convenience over the metal models that need assembly. It looks better than bare metal in a living room. The tradeoff is the rating, which is the lowest here, so it is for mid-weight pots, not urns.

Wood can suffer in standing water, so use a saucer on a wet patio. Compared with the Parsagi at 390 pounds, it carries about two thirds as much but is warmer looking and sold as a pair. Compared with the 600 pound MEADOMINGLE, it is for a different class of pot. A realistic scenario is a pair of matching 14 inch planters flanking a covered entry that you rotate for even light.
products.bestFor: Mid-weight indoor or covered-patio pots where appearance matters.
cons: Wood needs protection from standing water

buyingCriteria.explanation: Heavy-duty ratings in this guide run from 264 pounds on the IDZO to 600 pounds on the MEADOMINGLE, with the GLISWAM and TECHYANG at 500, the KEDSUM at 440 and the Parsagi at 390. Ratings describe a static load on a flat surface, and moving a loaded caddy over a threshold adds stress. Choose a rating at least 20 percent above the loaded weight of your pot. Wet soil and a large root ball weigh far more than most buyers expect.

More casters share the load, and more locks hold the pot still. The Parsagi lists five locking casters, the GLISWAM lists four locking, and the MEADOMINGLE has two lockable of four. The TECHYANG has nine wheels but its lock count is not stated in the bullets. For slopes, tile and busy corridors, prefer a caddy that locks every wheel.

Metal frames like the MEADOMINGLE, GLISWAM, KEDSUM and Parsagi are stiffest, and galvanizing or powder coating protects them outdoors. Plastic, as on the TECHYANG, resists rust and UV and is lighter. Wood such as the IDZO acacia looks best indoors but dislikes standing water. Match the material to the place where the pot will live.

A pot should sit fully on the platform, with a margin. The MEADOMINGLE is 22 inches for pots up to 24 inches, the TECHYANG is 20 inches, the KEDSUM is 16, the Parsagi is 14.5 outer and 13.6 inner, and the IDZO is 14. The GLISWAM adjusts from 21 to 30 inches. Measure the base of your pot, not the rim.

An adjustable frame like the GLISWAM covers square, rectangular and round pots and grows with your plant. A fixed tray is simpler and has fewer joints that can loosen. If you plan to repot into a larger planter, adjustable saves a second purchase. If your pot will not change, a fixed caddy is stiffer.

Some caddies arrive assembled, like the IDZO two-pack, while others need a wrench, like the Parsagi. Check fastener tightness on any assembled frame after the first few moves. Look for rust-resistant finishes if the caddy will sit on a wet deck. A quick check of every caster before loading the pot prevents surprises.

howWeEvaluated.title: Rated capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated ratings, from 264 pounds on the IDZO up to 600 pounds on the MEADOMINGLE. The GLISWAM and TECHYANG list 500, the KEDSUM 440 and the Parsagi 390. Picks scored higher where the rating matched the size and build.

howWeEvaluated.title: Casters and locks
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared caster counts and locks. The Parsagi has five locking casters and the GLISWAM four, while the MEADOMINGLE locks two of four. The TECHYANG has nine wheels but states no lock count, so we told readers to check the page.

howWeEvaluated.title: Frame and finish
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the frame materials and coatings: thickened metal, galvanized steel, UV plastic and acacia hardwood. We favored coatings stated in the listing and noted where the finish was not described.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and adjustability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared platform sizes from 14 to 22 inches and the GLISWAM adjustable range of 21 to 30 inches. We looked at whether the listing states the pot size each platform supports.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed the TECHYANG at a low price rank, the IDZO in the lower middle, the GLISWAM and Parsagi in the middle, the KEDSUM in the upper middle and the MEADOMINGLE at the top. Each was judged against its stated features.

cards.label: Fixed base
cards.text: A solid or fixed-size platform has fewer joints and stays stiff under load. Picks on this side are the MEADOMINGLE, TECHYANG, KEDSUM, Parsagi and IDZO. Choose one if your pot size will not change.

cards.text: An expandable frame like the GLISWAM spans 21 to 30 inches and fits square and round pots, but has more fasteners to check. Choose it if you will upsize planters or own several pot shapes.

cards.label: Which to pick
cards.text: If you own one large pot and it will not change, take a fixed caddy such as the MEADOMINGLE or Parsagi. If you repot every year or keep rectangular boxes, take the GLISWAM.

faq.q: How do I choose between the GLISWAM and the MEADOMINGLE?
faq.a: The GLISWAM adjusts from 21 to 30 inches, is rated 500 pounds and locks all four casters. The MEADOMINGLE is a fixed 22 inch platform rated 600 pounds with two of four casters locking. Choose the GLISWAM for flexibility and the MEADOMINGLE for the highest rating.

faq.q: Is 500 pounds enough for a large ceramic pot?
faq.a: Usually, but check the loaded weight first. A large ceramic pot with wet soil and a mature plant can weigh well over 200 pounds. Add a margin of about 20 percent. The TECHYANG, GLISWAM and MEADOMINGLE all list 500 pounds or more.

faq.q: Do more wheels make a caddy better?
faq.a: More wheels spread the load and roll more smoothly, as on the nine-wheel TECHYANG. But locks matter too, and the TECHYANG bullets do not state how many lock. A five-caster design like the Parsagi, with all five locking, can be more secure than a nine-wheel design with few locks.

faq.q: Will a metal caddy rust outdoors?
faq.a: It can if the finish is damaged. The KEDSUM is galvanized with an anti-rust coating, and the MEADOMINGLE is listed as rust-proof. Check for scratches after moving the caddy and keep it off standing water. Plastic like the TECHYANG does not rust.

faq.q: Can I use a heavy-duty caddy indoors?
faq.a: Yes, but protect the floor. Metal trays and hard wheels can scratch wood or tile if grit is trapped. Put a thin mat under the caddy and check that wheels roll freely. The IDZO acacia is a gentler-looking indoor choice.

faq.q: How do I move a loaded caddy safely?
faq.a: Unlock the wheels, push slowly and keep one hand on the pot. Avoid slopes and thresholds when possible, because they raise the tip risk. Lock every wheel once the pot is in position. For very heavy planters, ask for help.

faq.q: Is an adjustable caddy as strong as a solid one?
faq.a: Not always, because it has more fasteners and joints. The GLISWAM lists a cross-braced frame and a 500 pound rating, but you should tighten every fastener and recheck after early use. A fixed caddy like the Parsagi has fewer parts that can loosen.
